notes: Curated reference guide. Source dates and measurement uncertainties remain at the linked publications. Nearest-object descriptions are scoped to the cited population and report. No new catalog positions are invented.

metric.name: New Mexico State University · general relativity

10.title: A star powered by fusion
10.summary: Hydrogen fusion releases the energy that lights the solar system. The visible photosphere is a layer of plasma, not a solid surface.
10.detail: Rotation depends on latitude: the equator turns faster than the poles. A single rigid rotation speed would hide this important difference.

199.title: A world of long days
199.summary: Mercury completes three rotations for every two trips around the Sun. That spin–orbit resonance makes its solar day very different from its sidereal rotation period.
199.detail: Its thin exosphere offers little insulation between the sunlit and dark sides.

299.title: A slowly turning greenhouse world
299.summary: Venus turns in the retrograde direction. Its rotation relative to the stars takes longer than its orbit around the Sun.
299.detail: Its dense carbon-dioxide atmosphere traps heat. The bright cloud deck conceals the rocky surface.

399.title: A rotating ocean world
399.summary: Earth turns once relative to distant stars in about 23 hours 56 minutes. The familiar 24-hour solar day also includes our motion around the Sun.
399.detail: Equatorial rotation speed is roughly 1,674 km/h. Move the latitude control to see why the speed decreases toward the poles.

301.title: One face, a changing geometry
301.summary: The Moon rotates once per orbit around Earth, so it keeps approximately the same face toward us. Libration lets us see beyond one exact hemisphere over time.
301.detail: Its mean orbital distance is 384,400 km. The live distance below changes through the orbit; it is not that average.

499.title: A record of a wetter past
499.summary: Mars has a thin atmosphere and a cold, dusty surface. Channels and minerals preserve evidence that liquid water once altered this world.
499.detail: A Martian rotation is only a little longer than Earth’s. Its year is much longer because its orbit is farther from the Sun.

599.title: A giant with no solid surface
599.summary: Jupiter is dominated by hydrogen and helium. Bands, storms and its powerful magnetic environment make its visible atmosphere highly dynamic.
599.detail: The listed rotation is a reference period. Clouds at different latitudes do not all follow one rigid surface.

699.title: Ice rings around a gas giant
699.summary: Saturn’s rings contain enormous numbers of orbiting particles, mostly water ice. They are not a single solid disk.
699.detail: The reference rotation and radius describe the planet, not the orbital speed of the rings or a solid ground surface.

799.title: A planet tipped onto its side
799.summary: Uranus has an extreme axial tilt that produces unusual seasons. Methane in its atmosphere helps give it a blue-green appearance.
799.detail: The negative reference rotation period encodes retrograde rotation; the speed magnitude remains positive.

899.title: An active, distant ice giant
899.summary: Neptune’s atmosphere supports powerful winds and changing storms. Methane absorbs red light in its upper atmosphere.
899.detail: Reference surface textures are maps assembled from observations; cloud patterns are not being streamed live.

cards.title: Our nearest stellar neighbor
cards.name: Proxima Centauri
cards.text: Beyond the Sun, this faint red dwarf is the nearest star to us. Its light has traveled for more than four years before reaching Earth.
cards.detail: Distances are measured by observations such as parallax. The nearby-host map uses the dated NASA Exoplanet Archive snapshot and does not animate unmeasured planet phases.

cards.title: The nearest white dwarf
cards.name: Sirius B
cards.text: This compact stellar remnant accompanies Sirius A. A mass comparable to the Sun is packed into a body roughly Earth-sized.
cards.detail: A white dwarf no longer powers itself through ordinary core hydrogen fusion. Its glow comes from stored heat as it cools. Sirius B is a recorded observation, not a live 3D surface map.

cards.title: A nearby millisecond pulsar
cards.name: PSR J0437−4715
cards.text: NASA’s Fermi catalog lists a period of about 0.00576 seconds and a distance of 156.79 parsecs, approximately 511 light-years.
cards.detail: The 2024 NICER study describes it as the nearest observed millisecond pulsar. That is a specific class, not a claim that it is the nearest neutron star of any kind. Pulses arise as the rotating emission beam sweeps across our line of sight.

cards.title: A nearby dark companion
cards.name: Gaia BH1
cards.text: ESA identifies Gaia BH1 as the closest known black hole in its cited report. The motion of a visible companion reveals the unseen mass.
cards.detail: “Known” matters: discoveries can change rankings. A black hole need not have a bright accretion disk; absence of glowing gas does not mean absence of a black hole.

cards.title: Our galactic home
cards.name: Milky Way
cards.text: The solar system lies in the disk of a barred spiral galaxy. Looking toward the galactic center means looking through crowded star fields and dust.
cards.detail: We cannot photograph our entire galaxy from outside it. The overview reconstructs its large-scale structure; the decorative star points are not an all-star catalog.

cards.title: Nearest large galactic neighbor
cards.name: Andromeda · M31
cards.text: Andromeda is our nearest large galaxy. Its light gives us a view from roughly 2.5 million years ago.
cards.detail: It is not the nearest galaxy of every type: the Milky Way has much closer dwarf companions. “Nearest galaxy” needs a definition of the population being compared.

cards.title: Nucleus, pulsar, black hole
cards.name: Different things in space
cards.text: A galactic nucleus is the central region of a galaxy. A pulsar is a rotating neutron star seen through periodic emission. A black hole has an event horizon.
cards.detail: These words do not name the same object. Some galactic nuclei host an actively feeding supermassive black hole; many are comparatively quiet.

cards.title: Why gravity bends light
cards.name: Curved spacetime
cards.text: In general relativity, matter and energy influence spacetime geometry. Light follows that geometry, producing gravitational lensing.
cards.detail: A funnel drawing is an analogy, not a literal hole in a sheet. The relativity lab computes idealized clock rates and curvature for a spherical, nonrotating black hole.

cards.title: The orbit of light
cards.name: Photon sphere & stable orbits
cards.text: For the ideal nonrotating black hole, circular photon paths occur at 1.5 Schwarzschild radii. They are unstable. The innermost stable circular orbit for a test particle is at 3 Schwarzschild radii.
cards.detail: Spin changes these radii. A bright observed ring, the black-hole shadow and the event horizon are different structures.

cards.title: How far does a second reach?
cards.name: Light, distance & observation
cards.text: Light-travel time turns distance into a communication delay. The atlas calculates distance divided by the speed of light from simultaneous JPL positions.
cards.detail: Those numbers are geometric estimates. Precision signal timing also accounts for motion during the journey, relativity and observing geometry. Deep-space observations always show a past state.
